A retinue is a group of people who regularly accompany, assist, and serve one important or powerful person — wherever that person goes. Think of it as a personal team that travels with someone, specifically because that person is significant enough to need one.

The word is always used as a collective noun, meaning it refers to the whole group together, not any single member of it.
Breaking It Down — The Three Key Features

For a group to qualify as a retinue, three things are usually true:

1. There is one central, important figure.
The retinue exists because of this one person. That person is typically a leader, ruler, celebrity, or someone of high status — a king, a president, a pope, a powerful general, a famous musician. The retinue orbits around them.

2. The group accompanies that person.
A retinue doesn't stay at home. It moves with the important person — on journeys, to events, on official visits, on tours. Wherever the central figure goes, the retinue goes too.

3. The group serves or supports that person.
Each member of a retinue has a role that benefits the central figure. Some protect them. Some advise them. Some manage their affairs. Some attend to their personal comfort. Together, they make that person's life and work function smoothly.

Imagine a medieval king riding through his kingdom. He doesn't travel alone. Surrounding him is a large group: knights who protect him, servants who carry his belongings, advisors who counsel him, heralds who announce his arrival, and nobles who show their loyalty by accompanying him. That whole group — everyone riding with him in that official capacity — is his retinue.

Now fast-forward to today. A famous pop star arrives at an airport. Walking with them is a cluster of people: two bodyguards, a personal assistant managing their phone, a stylist carrying a bag of clothes, and a manager on a call. That cluster is the pop star's retinue.

The setting changes across history and culture, but the idea stays the same.
How It Is Used in Sentences

• "The ambassador arrived at the palace with a large retinue of diplomats and advisors."
  • "Wherever the emperor traveled, his retinue of servants and guards followed."
  • "The film director walked into the festival with her usual retinue — a producer, two assistants, and a publicist."
  • "He was used to traveling light, so the CEO's retinue of just three people surprised everyone."

Notice that you'll almost always see the phrase "a retinue of..." followed by a description of who is in the group. That is the most natural and common way to use the word.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

Retinue is a formal, somewhat literary word. It is not something you'd hear in casual everyday conversation. You wouldn't say, "I went to the party with my retinue." It would sound odd and grandiose.

You'll encounter it most often in:

  • Writing about history, royalty, or politics
  • News coverage of heads of state or major leaders
  • Formal or literary descriptions of powerful figures
  • Historical fiction and non-fiction

The word carries a sense of ceremony, prestige, and importance. When a writer uses "retinue," they are subtly signaling that the central person is significant — significant enough to have people whose entire purpose is to accompany and serve them.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Entourage is the closest modern equivalent and is often interchangeable with retinue. However, "entourage" feels more casual and is used heavily in pop culture (celebrities, athletes, influencers). "Retinue" sounds more formal and dignified — better suited for kings and presidents than for celebrities, though it can describe either.

Escort implies accompaniment and often protection, but it's usually a smaller group and doesn't carry the sense of an ongoing, established team the way "retinue" does.

Convoy refers specifically to vehicles traveling together, often for protection — it is about transportation, not people in a serving role.

So if you had to pick one distinction to remember: retinue = the personal team of attendants and supporters surrounding one important person, traveling with them and serving them.

A retinue can be small or enormous. A powerful medieval monarch might have hundreds of people in their retinue. A modern executive might travel with just two or three. The word itself doesn't specify a number — what matters is the relationship between the group and the central figure, not the headcount.
A retinue is the group of attendants, assistants, and supporters who accompany and serve one important person wherever they go.
